claims.statement: Attentional selection is usefully modeled as competition among goal-directed, stimulus-driven, and selection-history influences rather than a single salience process.
Reward-associated features can bias later attention, but traditional VDAC effects are weak and method-sensitive, so learned-value attention must not be assigned a universal large effect.
Sustained/vigilant attention is a distinct time-on-task problem and should not be collapsed into initial attentional capture.
Curiosity is not well represented by one information-gap mechanism; novelty, uncertainty, information gain, learning progress and other drives contribute to exploration.
Epistemic curiosity can involve appraisal of a knowledge gap, assignment of reward value to information, and motivation to seek knowledge.
Curiosity-driven exploration competes with other drives such as safety, so greater uncertainty is not guaranteed to increase exploration.
Cognitive appraisals show systematic relationships with differentiated emotions, but no single appraisal dimension explains emotion globally.
Valence is conceptually and operationally ambiguous across affective science, so valence must be defined rather than treated as a self-evident scalar.
Subjective value is a decision construct integrating utility/reward with context and uncertainty; it is related to but not identical with emotion.
Group identity can shape social influence through self-categorization and group norms, with strength depending on identification and context.
Anonymity versus visibility and isolation versus copresence can alter identity-based social influence, making online context a material moderator.
Social identity and self-categorization are related but non-identical theoretical components and should not be collapsed into generic similarity.

Trustworthiness, expertise and related source-credibility constructs are materially associated with influencer attitudinal and behavioral outcomes, but effect sizes vary by platform, geography, product and influencer type.
Experimental manipulation of heuristic source/social credibility cues has a small-to-moderate pooled effect on perceived credibility, with meaningful moderators.
Users can conflate source authenticity/credentials with message credibility, so credibility cues are not equivalent to accurate trust calibration.
Parasocial interaction and parasocial relationship should be represented as distinct but related constructs rather than one undifferentiated connection score.
Parasocial engagement is multidimensional, including cognitive, affective and behavioral dimensions, and its outcome relationships vary by product and content characteristics.
Parasocial associations vary by construct type, age and cultural region, so connection inference requires developmental and cultural context.
Social transmission is an observed communication behavior with multiple motives and moderators; audience, modality, channel and device can change what gets shared.
Specific emotion/arousal manipulations and field data have supported links between activation and online sharing in bounded contexts.
Two preregistered replications failed to find an effect of incidental physiological arousal on willingness to share news on social media, ruling out a universal arousal-to-sharing edge.
Habit is best distinguished from mere repetition or returning behavior: it involves learned context-response control and interfaces with, but is not identical to, goal-directed action.
Context-response associations can be measured separately from goal motivation, supporting a measurement distinction between habit mechanism and repeated behavior.
Prediction-error updating is a separable reinforcement-learning mechanism and should not be treated as synonymous with habit automaticity.
